title: Levels of CI
summary: Five levels of CI optimization, from the Actions cache to swapping runners, tuning workflows, switching CI engines, and replacing CI with agents.
body_markdown:
## How to think about making GitHub Actions cheaper and faster


Everyone is talking about CI these days. Anthropic's CI job volume[increased 25x over 6 months](https://claude.com/blog/agentic-coding-is-straining-ci-heres-how-we-scaled-test-impact-analysis-at-anthropic) while their tests[grew 10x](https://x.com/addyosmani/status/2099577600159158765) . Linear took up a major effort to[rework their CI](https://linear.app/now/ci-bottleneck-reworked) after their test suite[grew 3.7x](https://x.com/moofeez/status/2102110907295993918) . Meanwhile, more and more people are complaining about their GitHub Actions costs being out of control.


> “
>
>
> CI has become the top bottleneck of every engineering team I talk to (including Lindy). Our CI spend has become stratospheric. ”
>
>
> [Flo Crivello](https://x.com/Altimor/status/2104094039805174164) , founder of Lindy


We want to provide a practical guide, complete with agent docs and prompts, for how you should think about solving your CI bottleneck problem.


Like most problems, there's a spectrum of solutions you can adopt depending on how much of an investment you want to make.


CI cost is highly correlated with CI speed (since you get charged by the minute). If you want cheaper CI without taking a hit on speed, here's how to think about it.


## Level 0: make sure you're using Actions cache


This is the most basic of basic steps you need to take expeditiously if you haven't already (official docs[here](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching) ).


Cache dependencies Prompt for your coding agent


```text
Inspect this repo's .github/workflows for dependency caching. For every job that installs packages (npm, pnpm, yarn, pip, cargo, go, gradle, maven), check whether a cache is configured: a `cache:` key on `actions/setup-node` / `setup-python` / `setup-go`, an explicit `actions/cache` step, or a language-specific cache action. Flag any install step (`pnpm install`, `pip install`, `cargo build`, etc.) that has no matching cache restoring its store, and confirm the cache key is derived from the lockfile so it actually hits. Add the right cache hook keyed on the lockfile, then show me the diff and open a PR rather than applying it blindly.
```


Source:[Guide](https://starsling.dev/best-practices/github-actions/cache-dependencies#verify)


## Level 1: swap runners


Comparison of runners (including ours)[here](https://starsling.dev/compare) . If you're using GitHub-hosted Actions, swapping out runners is easy and you get faster and cheaper CI. Your workflows, triggers, and GitHub checks stay exactly as they are.


Migration prompt Prompt for your coding agent


```text
# Migrate GitHub Actions to StarSling Runners


Migrate the user's workflows from GitHub-hosted runners to StarSling Runners.


**Prerequisites:** `gh` CLI authenticated, [StarSling GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/starslingdev) installed on the repo's org.


## Configuration


**Target:** `starsling-ubuntu-24.04` | **Branch:** `migrate-starsling-ubuntu-2404`


**Source runners to replace:** `ubuntu-latest`, `ubuntu-24.04`


Replace all UPPERCASE placeholders (`OWNER`, `REPO`, `BRANCH_NAME`, `HEAD_OID`, `BASE64_CONTENT`, `FILE_NAME`, `N`, `DEFAULT_BRANCH`) with actual values from previous steps.


## Procedure


### Step 1: Confirm GitHub App Installation


Ask the user: "Have you installed the [StarSling GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/starslingdev) on your org? It's required for runners to pick up jobs after merge. If not, please install it first and let me know when you're ready."


**Do not run any commands or proceed to Step 2 until the user explicitly confirms the app is installed.**


### Step 2: Verify CLI Auth


Verify `gh auth status` succeeds. If not, direct the user to install from https://cli.github.com/ and run `gh auth login`.


### Step 3: Get Repository


Ask the user for the repository (`owner/repo`). Then run `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO --jq '.owner.type'`. If the result is `User` (not `Organization`), stop and explain: "StarSling Runners only work with GitHub organization repositories. You can create a free organization at https://github.com/account/organizations/new."


### Step 4: Discover Workflows


Fetch all workflow files in one API call:


```bash
cat <<'QUERY' | gh api graphql --input -
{
"query": "query($owner: String!, $repo: String!) { repository(owner: $owner, name: $repo) { id nameWithOwner defaultBranchRef { name target { oid } } object(expression: \"HEAD:.github/workflows\") { ... on Tree { entries { name object { ... on Blob { text } } } } } } }",
"variables": { "owner": "OWNER", "repo": "REPO" }
}
QUERY
```


Note: `HEAD` in the GraphQL expression is a Git ref, not a placeholder - do not replace it.


If the response is truncated or errors due to size, fall back to the REST API: fetch the default branch and HEAD SHA via `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO --jq '.default_branch'` and `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/git/ref/heads/DEFAULT_BRANCH --jq '.object.sha'`, then fetch workflow file names via `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/contents/.github/workflows` and each file individually via `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/contents/.github/workflows/FILE_NAME`. The response `content` field is base64-encoded - decode it before scanning for `runs-on:` values.


Save `defaultBranchRef.name` (or REST default branch), `.target.oid` / HEAD SHA, and workflow `entries[]`. Scan each `.yml`/`.yaml` file for:
- direct `runs-on:` string values matching supported runners, and
- matrix-driven patterns (e.g., `runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}`) where the matrix values include supported runner labels.


Show the user a summary including:
- Workflows that will be migrated and which runners are being replaced
- Any Ubuntu runners NOT in the supported list (e.g., `ubuntu-22.04`, `ubuntu-20.04`, larger runners like `ubuntu-latest-16-cores`) listed as "Not migrated - unsupported runner label"


If no direct or matrix-backed supported runners match, stop.


### Step 5: Preview Changes


**Never create a PR without the user confirming changes first.**


Show what will change per workflow:
- Replace supported runners in `runs-on:` string values with `starsling-ubuntu-24.04` (preserve quotes/comments)
- Replace matching `runner:`/`os:` values in `matrix.include` sections
- Skip commented lines


**Complex `runs-on` patterns:**
- **Array syntax** (e.g., `runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, ubuntu-latest]`): Only replace the matching label within the array; do not collapse to a single string
- **Group/labels syntax** (e.g., `runs-on: { group: ..., labels: [...] }`): Skip and flag for manual review
- **Expressions** (`${{ matrix.os }}`, ternary/conditional): If `runs-on` uses `${{ matrix.os }}` and the matrix values are hardcoded runner labels, replace the labels in the matrix definition and flag the workflow for manual verification. If the matrix values come from other expressions, skip entirely and flag for manual review


**YAML fidelity:** Change ONLY the `runs-on` and matrix values. Preserve the original file exactly: same indentation, key ordering, comments, blank lines, and trailing newline. The PR diff should show only the runner label changes.


### Step 6: Create PR


**Branch:** Before creating, check for existing branches: `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/git/matching-refs/heads/migrate-starsling-ubuntu-2404 --jq '.[].ref'`. If any exist, find the highest numeric suffix and increment by 1 (if none have a suffix, use `-2`). Then create: `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/git/refs -f ref=refs/heads/BRANCH_NAME -f sha=HEAD_OID`.


**Atomic commit** - all files in one commit, contents base64-encoded:


```bash
cat <<'MUTATION' | gh api graphql --input -
{
"query": "mutation($input: CreateCommitOnBranchInput!) { createCommitOnBranch(input: $input) { commit { oid url } } }",
"variables": {
"input": {
"branch": {
"repositoryNameWithOwner": "OWNER/REPO",
"branchName": "BRANCH_NAME"
},
"message": {
"headline": "Migrate N CI workflows to StarSling Runners",
"body": "Replaced runners per file:\n- file1.yml: ubuntu-latest → starsling-ubuntu-24.04\n- file2.yml: ubuntu-24.04 → starsling-ubuntu-24.04"
},
"expectedHeadOid": "HEAD_OID",
"fileChanges": {
"additions": [
{ "path": ".github/workflows/FILE_NAME", "contents": "BASE64_CONTENT" }
]
}
}
}
}
MUTATION
```


Verify the response contains a valid `commit.oid`. If the mutation returned an `expectedHeadOid` mismatch, re-fetch the HEAD SHA (Step 4) and retry the commit once. For any other errors, report and stop - do not create a PR against a failed commit.


**Commit message:** The headline should read `Migrate N CI workflows to StarSling Runners` where N is the count of modified workflow files (`.yml` + `.yaml`). List each file and the runner label(s) replaced in the body, as shown in the example above.


**PR** via `gh pr create --repo OWNER/REPO --head BRANCH_NAME --base DEFAULT_BRANCH --title "Migrate N CI workflows to StarSling Runners" --body "..."` with this body structure:


```
## Summary
Migrates CI workflows from GitHub-hosted runners to [StarSling Runners](https://docs.starsling.dev) for faster builds and AI-powered optimizations and fixes.


## Changes
- \`file1.yml\`: \`ubuntu-latest\` → \`starsling-ubuntu-24.04\`
- \`file2.yml\`: \`ubuntu-24.04\` → \`starsling-ubuntu-24.04\`


## Not Migrated
- \`file3.yml\`: Uses \`${{ matrix.os }}\` - requires manual review
(or "All workflows migrated successfully.")


## After Merging
Workflows will automatically run on StarSling Runners. Ensure the [StarSling GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/starslingdev) is installed with access to this repo.
```


### Step 7: Monitor (Optional)


Ask the user if they'd like help monitoring after merge. If yes, explain they can return after merging and you'll check with:


```bash
gh run list --repo OWNER/REPO --branch DEFAULT_BRANCH --limit 5 --json status,conclusion,name,createdAt
```


Look for runs created after the merge. If any show `queued` for more than 2 minutes, suggest checking the GitHub App installation and repo access at https://github.com/apps/starslingdev.


## Error Handling


| Error | Solution |
|-------|----------|
| `gh` not found or not logged in | Install from https://cli.github.com/, run `gh auth login` |
| 403 / insufficient permissions | User needs write access to the repository - check collaborator status or org role |
| App not installed | Install from https://github.com/apps/starslingdev |
| Personal repo (owner type `User`) | StarSling requires an org repo - create one at https://github.com/account/organizations/new |
| Repository not found | Check repo name and permissions |
| No workflows found | Ensure `.github/workflows/` exists |
| Runner not available after merge | Verify app has repo access at https://github.com/apps/starslingdev |
| Rate limit exceeded | Wait a few minutes and retry |
| 422 on branch creation | Branch exists - append a number suffix |
| `expectedHeadOid` mismatch | Re-fetch HEAD SHA and retry the commit |
| `${{ matrix.os }}` / complex `runs-on` | Require manual review - determined at runtime |
| GraphQL response truncated | Fall back to REST API for individual file fetches |
```


Source:[StarSling Runners](https://starsling.dev/products/runners)


## Level 2: optimize your tests and workflows


Our guides cover the fixes that make the biggest difference in most repos: caching dependencies and builds, splitting long test suites across parallel jobs, skipping work a change can't affect, and cancelling runs a newer push has replaced. Each one comes with a prompt your agent can run against your repo and a way to verify the fix.


Check out our guides ([18 best practices](https://starsling.dev/best-practices/github-actions) ,[16 optimization recipes](https://starsling.dev/github-actions/optimizations) ) or give your agent the prompts below.


CI cost breakdown Prompt for your coding agent


```text
Show me where my CI minutes and money go, across every runner provider I use, as a table ranked from most to least. Use the authenticated gh CLI. Read only: change nothing until I approve.


1. GitHub's bill. Get the owner from gh repo view --json owner (ask me only outside a repo or for an enterprise; query no other account). Select exactly one prefix: organizations/ORG, enterprises/ENTERPRISE, or users/USERNAME; then run gh api "/<selected-prefix>/settings/billing/usage?year=YYYY&month=M" for the last full month. From usageItems keep the Actions minutes and storage: netAmount (billed after included usage), quantity, unitType, by repositoryName and sku. On 403 or 404, re-run with gh api -i and give me the gh auth refresh -h github.com -s <scope> named in X-Accepted-OAuth-Scopes (fine-grained tokens need Administration (read) for an org or Plan (read) for a user; enterprises need a classic token).


2. Minutes on every runner, for the same month as the bill (created=YYYY-MM-01..YYYY-MM-DD on every runs call), in this order, within about 500 API calls in total. (a) Find the runners first: list the owner's repos (gh repo list OWNER --limit 1000 --json name,pushedAt), keep those with runs that month, and read their workflow files' runs-on labels. Map each label to a provider: GitHub-hosted (ubuntu-*, windows-*, macos-*, and larger runners matched to the bill's SKUs), StarSling (starsling-*), Blacksmith (blacksmith-*), Depot (depot-*), Namespace (namespace-profile-*), WarpBuild (warp-*), RunsOn (contains runs-on= or starts runs-on/), BuildJet (buildjet-*), otherwise self-hosted. (b) Sample next, up to about 250 calls, choosing sample sizes before the first call so the total fits: every workflow that ran gets at least one completed run from that month, then the busiest get up to about 10, each with its jobs (gh api "/repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs/RUN_ID/jobs?filter=all&per_page=100" --paginate). Bill each job as completed_at minus started_at, rounded up to the minute, confirm its provider from the job's labels, and record average billed minutes per run. (c) Count last, up to about 150 calls: one call per workflow (gh api "/repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/workflows/WORKFLOW_FILE/runs?created=RANGE&per_page=1" --jq .total_count). GitHub caps this count at 2,500; when it reads 2,500, do not split the range, estimate the month from the sample's runs per day instead. A workflow's monthly minutes are its run count times its average billed minutes per run, per runner. For GitHub-hosted runners the bill already has each repository's exact total: use these minutes only to split that total across the repository's workflows. If the budget runs out, still show every provider found, with what is known, marked as an estimate.


3. Prices. GitHub-hosted: the bill's netAmount is exact. StarSling: read https://starsling.dev/pricing.md, which maps each label to its price. Every other provider: estimate a range from GitHub's list rate for the same machine size, from half that rate to the full rate, using https://docs.github.com/api/article/body?pathname=/en/billing/reference/actions-runner-pricing, and label it an estimate. Self-hosted: minutes only, no price.


4. The answer. Start with a short summary: total CI spend and total runner minutes for the month, then one line per provider found (minutes and dollars, each marked exact or estimate; list only providers that ran jobs), then the share of the total that is exact. Anywhere in the answer, mention only providers that ran jobs, never ones that did not or that appear only in workflow files. Next, one table of the top 5 workflows ranked by runner minutes per month, highest first: repository, workflow, provider and runner, minutes per month, and dollars per month, with each figure marked exact or estimate. Put every other workflow in one row below them, with its count and totals. Exact: GitHub-hosted totals per repository and storage, both from the bill. Estimate: GitHub-hosted totals split across workflows, and all minutes and dollars on every other provider, because GitHub records those jobs but does not bill them (run counts are exact, run lengths are sampled). Add storage (artifacts and caches) from the bill as its own rows. Then the same totals by repository, and a line saying what share of the total is exact. Keep included minutes in mind: GitHub charges only for minutes above the plan's allowance, so one fix can remove more than its own row.


5. Then offer these drill-downs and wait for me to pick: (a) exact prices for my other providers, which you read from each vendor's live pricing page, (b) the jobs inside the workflows with the most minutes, (c) runs repeated on a commit that already passed, and the skip condition that let them through, (d) storage: the largest artifacts and which have no expiry, (e) the smallest set of workflow changes that removes the most spend, with dollars saved each, (f) what each row would cost on StarSling. Wait for my approval before editing anything.
```


Source:[GitHub Actions pricing](https://starsling.dev/github-actions-pricing#cost-prompt)


Why CI is slow Prompt for your coding agent


```text
Inspect the most recent slow GitHub Actions run and separate the wait before each job starts from the time the job spends executing steps. Pull the workflow run and its jobs from the Actions REST API. Report total pre-start delay as each job's started_at minus the workflow run's created_at. To adjust a job with needs dependencies, read the workflow file at the run's head_sha, then map each YAML job ID to its runtime job rows, accounting for an explicit name and every matrix expansion. Only when that mapping is unambiguous, compare the downstream started_at with the latest completed_at among every runtime row for its direct upstream jobs. Otherwise report total pre-start delay without claiming a precise dependency-adjusted queue time. Then group execution time by checkout, dependency install, build, tests, Docker, deploy, and fixed sleeps. Decide whether the dominant cause is dependency wait, runner queueing, runner hardware, or workflow waste. For each cause, propose the smallest safe fix, link it to the exact workflow lines, and say what measurement would prove the fix worked. Do not rewrite CI syntax or weaken required checks. Open one focused PR only if the evidence points to a clear fix.
```


Source:[GitHub Actions too slow](https://starsling.dev/github-actions-too-slow#agent-prompt)


Full catalog of optimizations Prompt for your coding agent


```text
Fetch https://starsling.dev/github-actions/catalog.json and read it. For each rule whose detectionMode is "static", fetch the markdown URL and run the page's detection steps against this repository. List every rule that applies, ordered by likely impact, with the file and line behind each finding. For "runtime" rules, list what run history you would need from the GitHub Actions API. A "hybrid" rule is both: run its detection steps against the repository AND name the run history that would confirm it. Then propose fixes for the top findings and open them as a reviewable PR; do not apply changes blindly.
```


Source:[Optimization recipes](https://starsling.dev/github-actions/optimizations)


There are also a lot of skills out there that can help you with this, including ours:


- [ci-speedup](https://github.com/starslingdev/skills/blob/main/skills/ci-speedup/SKILL.md) (StarSling,[skill page](https://starsling.dev/skills/ci-speedup) )
- [ci-score](https://github.com/starslingdev/skills/blob/main/skills/ci-score/SKILL.md) (StarSling,[skill page](https://starsling.dev/skills/ci-score) )
- [ci-cd-and-automation](https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/ci-cd-and-automation/SKILL.md) (Addy Osmani, Anthropic)
- [test-audit](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/.agents/skills/test-audit/SKILL.md) (Peter Steinberger, OpenClaw)


Run ci-speedup Prompt for your coding agent


```text
Run `npx skills use "https://github.com/starslingdev/skills" --skill "ci-speedup"` and follow the generated skill instructions now. Read its complete output, redirecting it to a temporary file first if necessary. Resolve relative paths from the supporting-files directory it provides.
```


Source:[ci-speedup](https://starsling.dev/skills/ci-speedup)


StarSling Runners have optimizations built-in so you don't need to be in the loop, you just wake up to PRs. You can see example PRs that StarSling agents have shipped[here](https://starsling.dev/products/runners#ai-prs) .


## Level 3: switch CI engines


The next best way to make CI extremely fast is to run *far* fewer tests on each PR. That requires moving off of GitHub Actions and onto a custom engine so you can get more aggressive caching and test selection.


So what is a custom CI engine? If you're using GitHub Actions (GHA), that is the engine. Your workflow files and the syntax for them execute with the[GitHub Actions Runner](https://github.com/actions/runner) . The GitHub Actions Runner can run jobs in parallel, but[until recently](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-25-actions-steps-can-now-be-run-in-parallel/) couldn't run steps in parallel. You also can't use the output from steps across jobs without writing to the GitHub Actions cache or artifacts store.


CI is a solved problem at many mature tech companies. Meta and Google built their own build systems,[Buck2](https://buck2.build/) and Blaze (open-sourced as[Bazel](https://bazel.build/) ). The key feature of these engines is aggressive caching and test selection so that CI only runs tests that are relevant for the code change in the PR. This is how hyperscalers like them have managed to have massive monorepos with thousands of daily contributors without having CI become a bottleneck.


Now that agents write most of the code at an order of magnitude higher volume, companies that are at a fraction of the size of the hyperscalers are experiencing the pains of having CI that runs the full suite on every PR.


So once you've done the oil change (faster runners) and tuning (optimizations), the only way to get truly more speed is to swap out the engine itself.


Adopting a new CI engine isn't easy, though. Unlike switching runners, which can be as simple as changing a` runs-on` label, moving to a new engine often means changing how your CI is defined and maintained. In a large monorepo, that can mean introducing new configuration for individual packages or services, keeping those definitions in sync as the repo changes, and retraining developers on a new CI model. That creates a much higher barrier to entry.


The payoff is that a custom CI engine has control over the entire execution layer, not just the machines running your jobs. It can make smarter decisions about what to run, parallelize work more aggressively, improve caching and scheduling, and remove overhead that GitHub Actions itself controls. Some CI engines claim they can run existing GitHub Actions workflows 10x faster.


So the tradeoff is straightforward: runners are much easier to adopt, but a new CI engine gives you a much larger surface area to optimize.


If you want a custom CI engine, there are a handful of popular options:


- [Dagger](https://dagger.io/)
- [Buildkite](https://buildkite.com/) ([GHA-compatible](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/migration/run-github-actions-workflows) )
- [Depot CI](https://depot.dev/products/ci) ([GHA-compatible](https://depot.dev/docs/ci/overview) )
- [CircleCI](https://circleci.com/)
- [GitLab CI](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/)


If you're thinking of adopting[Cursor Origin](https://cursor.com/changelog/origin-code-hosting) , you'll need to adopt a new CI engine to have CI running there.


At StarSling, we're working on our own custom CI engine that will be agent-native (works really well with your agents, similar to[sling](https://starsling.dev/cli) ). Sign up for early access if you're interested in trying it out **[here](https://tally.so/r/pb87xV)** .


## Level 4: throw out CI engines entirely


> “
>
>
> I have a suggestion: don't run CI ”
>
>
> [kache](https://x.com/yacineMTB/status/2104388490288857256)


This is the most extreme approach. No more CI. Meaning, no full suite of deterministic tests and builds that run in your codebase on every PR. There are a few approaches[being discussed](https://x.com/auchenberg/status/2104339748408229948) for what this could mean:


**1. Agent driven test selection.** Peter from OpenClaw is planning on letting Codex handle test selection:


> “
>
>
> My plan is to let codex decide which tests actually need to run and drastically nix CI and run tests hourly. ”
>
>
> [Peter Steinberger](https://x.com/steipete/status/2104305554760114488) , creator of OpenClaw


**2. CI after merge with auto-remediation.** This approach doesn't run CI at all before PRs merge and accepts risk of regressions on the main branch. Instead the full test suite runs continuously and an LLM is in the loop to catch and auto-remediate failures.


> “
>
>
> have something that is running actual functional tests off of your master branch on a cron, and then if any regressions occur, automatically have an LLM bisect and figure out the bug and then patch it... ”
>
>
> [kache](https://x.com/yacineMTB/status/2104388708694634544)


**3. Agents replace CI.** We believe that the future of code verification is an agent that replaces the function of CI. Instead of deterministic builds or tests an agent can simply ask another agent "is this code good?". The code verification agent might use scripts or create custom tests just-in-time for that specific change. Meta has promising research in this direction:[The Death of Traditional Testing](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/02/11/developer-tools/the-death-of-traditional-testing-agentic-development-jit-testing-revival/) .


Earlier this year, this wouldn't have even been possible. But now that tokens are getting cheaper by the day, this is a real possibility. We think that's the future.


If CI cost is top of mind for you, determine which level you're at and adopt the right strategy accordingly. Most companies are somewhere between Level 1 and 2 so there's still plenty of opportunity to improve. You just have to decide how much time and money you want to throw at the problem.
